newsitem.title: CANADA: Queen Elizabeth marks Canada's confederation.
newsitem.headline: Queen Elizabeth marks Canada's confederation.

text.p: Queen Elizabeth, Canada's head of state, helped celebrate the country's 130th birthday on Tuesday in her last major public appearance of a 10-day visit.
She and Prince Philip arrived on Parliament Hill in a horse-drawn landau to a 21-gun salute to give a speech marking Canada Day, the anniversary of Canada's confederation in 1867.

The queen had dispatched her son, Prince Charles, to hand over power in Hong Kong to the Chinese while she toured Canada, where she is likely to remain head of state for some time due partly to the affection with which many regard her and also to the difficulty of amending the constitution.

"I urge you now, all of you, to recognise how precious this country is and how much you have accomplished together, as a community of different peoples, living and growing together," she said in an address to the nation.
She was escorted to Parliament Hill with a musical salute by scarlet-uniformed Foot Guards, sweltering in their trademark tall bear-fur hats.
Underlying talk of Canadian unity in the midst of diversity is the constant thought of preventing French-speaking Quebec from leaving the confederation as separatists want.
Francophone Prime Minister Jean Chretien extolled a Canada where "diversity and pluralism are a source of strength and unity, not conflict and division."
The royal couple, who on Tuesday afternoon were to cut a 100-foot (30 metre) cake marking their 50th anniversary, were scheduled to fly home on Wednesday.
